writing.title: Writing 4: Reflect and Improve
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Return to your contrast paragraph from Writing 2 and improve it using the unit checklist: confirm you used at least two contrast conjunctions correctly, check the commas after opening although-clauses and while-clauses, replace two weak words with precise unit vocabulary, and proofread spelling. Then write a reflection of two paragraphs naming the changes you made, quoting one sentence before and after the change, and explaining which checklist item helped you most and why.
writing.modelText: Before: People today believe things fast. After: While readers once waited for the evening news, people today accept a rumour before lunch. The checklist item on contrast conjunctions helped me most, because it forced my two ideas to meet in one sentence.
writing.sentenceStarter: The first change I made was...
writing.expectedLength: The revised paragraph plus two reflection paragraphs

items: Revised paragraph: Communication has changed dramatically since our grandparents were young. Although people once wrote long letters and waited weeks for a reply, a message today reaches its reader in seconds. While face-to-face conversation demanded real courtesy, a video call lets someone look away without consequence. Whereas the radio broadcast only what conventional editors had checked, social media rewards whoever posts first, and gullible readers rarely stop to ask who wrote the claim. This speed has traded shrewd caution for the pervasive urgency of the present.

Reflection paragraph 1 (changes made): I made three main changes to my paragraph. First, I checked my contrast conjunctions and kept although, while and whereas, since all three were used correctly to link opposing ideas. Second, I added a comma after each opening although-clause and while-clause; for example, my sentence 'Although people once wrote long letters and waited weeks for a reply a message today reaches its reader in seconds' became 'Although people once wrote long letters and waited weeks for a reply, a message today reaches its reader in seconds.' Third, I replaced two weak words with more precise unit vocabulary, swapping 'a lot' for 'dramatically' and 'easily-fooled' for 'gullible'.

Reflection paragraph 2 (most helpful checklist item): The checklist item that helped me most was replacing weak words with precise vocabulary, because it forced me to think about exactly what I meant instead of writing the first phrase that came to mind. Changing 'huge rush' to 'pervasive urgency' made my final sentence sound far more serious and controlled, which matched the point I was trying to make about how quickly false stories can spread today.

writing.title: Writing 5: Sentence Building Portfolio
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Build a portfolio of ten sentences that shows your control of this unit's grammar: one sentence with although contrasting two ideas about school life; one with while comparing two people's opinions; one with whereas contrasting two places; one with a gerund as subject and one with a gerund as object; one present continuous sentence describing something happening at your school right now; one sentence using the abstract noun serenity or foresight; one conversion of this line into reported speech: Sami said, "I will check the source before I share it."; one zero conditional fact about communication; and one first conditional warning about spreading rumours. Then choose your best four sentences and arrange them into a short connected paragraph.
writing.modelText: Although our corridor noticeboard is small, it starts the biggest conversations. Checking a source takes two minutes, whereas rebuilding lost trust can take a year. Sami said that he would check the source before he shared it.
writing.expectedLength: Ten portfolio sentences and one connected paragraph

items: 1) although, contrasting two ideas about school life: Although our lunch break is short, it is the busiest part of the school day.
2) while, comparing two people's opinions: While Amal thinks the flyer should have been reported straight away, Nora believes the class should have investigated it first.
3) whereas, contrasting two places: The library stays hushed and orderly, whereas the canteen is loud and unpredictable.
4) gerund as subject: Checking a source properly takes less time than most students expect.
5) gerund as object: Teacher Yasmin recommends verifying every claim before repeating it.
6) present continuous, something happening at school right now: Right now, a group of students is reading the noticeboard outside the staffroom.
7) abstract noun (foresight): Sami's foresight in double-checking the flyer's source saved the class from repeating a false story.
8) reported speech conversion of Sami said, "I will check the source before I share it.": Sami said that he would check the source before he shared it.
9) zero conditional fact about communication: If a source cannot be named, a claim is not yet a fact.
10) first conditional warning about spreading rumours: If students share a rumour without checking it, they will damage their own credibility.

Connected paragraph (best four sentences, 4, 7, 8 and 10): Checking a source properly takes less time than most students expect, yet it is the habit that matters most before anything is repeated. Sami's foresight in double-checking the flyer's source saved the class from repeating a false story, and Sami said that he would check the source before he shared it long before the flyer became a problem. If students share a rumour without checking it, they will damage their own credibility, so that single habit of checking first is worth the extra minute every time.

writing.title: Writing 6: News Report on the Hoax Protest
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a short news report of 150 to 200 words about the hoax protest in Whispers Beyond the Gate, as it might appear in the local news outlet that exposed the truth. Give the report a concise headline, open with a factual first sentence saying what happened and where, and use reported speech at least three times to relay what Amal, Nora and Teacher Yasmin said — no direct quotations allowed. End with one sentence about the Student Forum the school created afterwards. Keep the tone neutral and factual, unlike the flyer that started the trouble.
writing.modelText: Students misled by hoax flyer, forum founded in response. A crowd of teenagers blocked Harbour Road on Tuesday after an anonymous flyer claimed the port was closing. One student organiser said that the school had lost trust before it lost anything else.
writing.sentenceStarter: A crowd of teenagers blocked Harbour Road after...
writing.expectedLength: A headline and three short paragraphs

items: Headline: Hoax Flyer Sparks Harbour Road Protest, Prompts New Student Forum

Paragraph 1 (factual opening): A crowd of teenagers blocked Harbour Road on Tuesday morning after an anonymous flyer wrongly claimed that the town's port was closing within the week. Local shopkeepers reported that dozens of students had gathered before the first lesson bell, and lessons across the school were delayed by nearly an hour.

Paragraph 2 (reported speech from Amal, Nora and Teacher Yasmin, no direct quotations): Amal said that she had shared the flyer because it looked plausible, but later admitted that she had not checked who had written it. Nora explained that the class had traced the flyer back to an account with no real name attached to it. Teacher Yasmin told reporters that the protest only happened because nobody had asked a single question about the source before believing it.

Paragraph 3 (closing, on the Student Forum): In response, the school announced that a new Student Forum would meet weekly to review claims before they spread, giving students a structured place to check facts together instead of arguing outside the gates. The head teacher confirmed that the forum's first meeting would take place before the end of term.

activities.instructionsAndItems: Fill each blank with although, while or whereas, then rewrite two of the sentences with the clause order reversed: 1) ______ Maya prefers reading fiction, her brother enjoys non-fiction books. 2) ______ the weather was very hot, the students continued their outdoor activity. 3) The harbour district is busy and loud, ______ the old town stays quiet. 4) ______ some people believe everything they read online, others are more sceptical. 5) She worked very hard on the project, ______ the final result was disappointing. 6) Traditional markets are lively and social, ______ online shopping is convenient but impersonal. 7) ______ the exam was difficult, most students managed to pass. 8) Daniel likes to plan everything in advance, ______ Maya is more spontaneous.

activities.title: Activities 2: Reported Speech Newsroom
activities.instructionsAndItems: You are the school newspaper's reporter. Convert each direct quotation into reported speech for your article, changing tenses, pronouns and time expressions: 1) Nora said, "I am proud of the student forum." 2) Daniel said, "We will check the facts before we share anything." 3) Teacher Yasmin asked, "Have you finished your homework?" 4) Sami said, "I did not share the flyer." 5) Maya said, "I was reading the article when the bell rang." activities.title: Activities 3: Vocabulary Detective
activities.instructionsAndItems: Round one — match each word to its definition: 1) embargo, 2) pensive, 3) shrewd, 4) concede, 5) spontaneous, 6) pervasive, 7) longevity, 8) squalor. Definitions: a) thinking deeply in a sad or serious way; b) a law that stops trade; c) to admit something is true after resisting; d) having good judgement and making smart decisions; e) spreading widely; f) happening suddenly without planning; g) very dirty conditions; h) how long something lives or lasts. Round two — find the odd one out in each group and explain why: 9) serenity, foresight, barricade, defiance. 10) shrewd, gullible, conscientious, embargo. 11) allot, assimilate, concise, dispel. 12) plausible, bizarre, conventional, cite.

activities.title: Activities 4: Conditional Logic Lab
activities.instructionsAndItems: For each sentence, write the correct verb forms and label it zero or first conditional: 1) If you ______ (mix) truth with rumour, people ______ (become) confused. 2) If Amal ______ (check) the source, she ______ (find) out the truth. 3) If water ______ (reach) one hundred degrees, it ______ (boil). 4) If we ______ (not think) critically, we ______ (fall) for misinformation. Answers: 1) mix / become -- zero conditional. 2) checks / will find -- first conditional. 3) reaches / boils -- zero conditional. 4) do not think / will fall -- first conditional. grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Languages and Communication" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 12-13 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'concise'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "The Speed of a Whisper: How Rumours Travel" was about in their own words, and what happened in "Whispers Beyond the Gate, part 1" — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "Contrast Conjunctions: Although, While and Whereas" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.

sections.title: Sentence Patterns to Say Out Loud
items: Although it was raining, the students played outside. She passed the exam although she had not studied much.
Reading improves your vocabulary.

She felt a deep serenity watching the sunset.
Close the door.

sections.title: Simple Check — What to Look For
sections.body: You do not need a test. These are the signs the unit has landed — listen for them in conversation and look for them in the writing:
items: Vocabulary use and comprehension responses
Grammar, speaking and activity performance
Independent writing, presentation or project evidence
